This vignette compares national income tax schedules with the tables that ship
with calcbloc. Everything below runs offline: no API key and no network.

Data by CalcBloc ([calcbloc.com/data](https://calcbloc.com/data?utm_source=calcbloc-r&utm_medium=docs&utm_campaign=itmarkerz-oss)), CC BY 4.0.
Every row carries the official source it was taken from (`source_url`), the
date it was retrieved and its verification status.

```{r}
library(calcbloc)
```

## Find the band schedules

`cb_countries()` lists what is bundled; `cb_sections()` lists the sections of
one table. Sections of kind `"bands"` are progressive schedules: rows with
`from`, `to` and `rate`.

```{r}
cs <- cb_countries()
cs[, c("country", "currency", "current_year", "last_verified")]

us <- cb_tax_table("us")
cb_sections(us, kind = "bands")[, c("section_id", "rows", "basis")]
```

The `basis` column matters: it says which amount the bands apply to. US federal
brackets apply to taxable income (after the standard or itemised deduction);
UK bands apply to taxable income above the Personal Allowance; Australian
rates apply to the whole of taxable income, with a 0% first band.

## A side-by-side summary

We pick the main schedule of eight countries: the federal schedule for the US
and Canada (provincial tax comes on top), the resident schedule for Australia,
the new (default) regime for India.

```{r}
schedules <- data.frame(
  country = c("us", "uk", "canada", "australia", "india", "singapore", "austria", "italy"),
  section = c("federal-income-tax-single", "income-tax-england", "federal-income-tax",
              "resident-rates", "new-regime", "income-tax", "income-tax", "irpef"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
tables <- lapply(schedules$country, cb_tax_table)
names(tables) <- schedules$country

summary_row <- function(tab, section) {
  b <- tab[tab$section_id == section, ]
  b <- b[order(b$from), ]
  data.frame(
    country = attr(tab, "country"),
    year = attr(tab, "year_label"),
    currency = attr(tab, "currency"),
    bands = nrow(b),
    lowest_rate = min(b$rate),
    top_rate = max(b$rate),
    top_rate_from = b$from[which.max(b$rate)],
    source = b$source_url[1],
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}
overview <- do.call(rbind, Map(summary_row, tables, schedules$section))
rownames(overview) <- NULL
overview[, -8]
```

The `source` column holds the official publication for each schedule:

```{r}
cat(sprintf("%-10s %s", overview$country, overview$source), sep = "\n")
```

## Marginal and average rates

`cb_tax_from_bands()` is vectorised, so a whole income grid goes in at once,
and `cb_marginal_rate()` gives the rate of the band each income falls in. The
incomes are in each country's own currency, so each panel has its own x axis.

```{r rates, fig.height = 8}
op <- par(mfrow = c(4, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1), cex = 0.7)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(schedules))) {
  tab <- tables[[i]]
  sec <- schedules$section[i]
  top <- max(tab$from[tab$section_id == sec], na.rm = TRUE)
  income <- seq(0, 2 * top, length.out = 400)
  avg <- ifelse(income > 0, cb_tax_from_bands(income, tab, sec) / income, 0)
  marg <- cb_marginal_rate(income, tab, sec)
  plot(income, 100 * marg, type = "s", ylim = c(0, 60), col = "grey40",
       xlab = paste("Income,", attr(tab, "currency")), ylab = "Rate (%)",
       main = paste(attr(tab, "country_name"), attr(tab, "year_label")))
  lines(income, 100 * avg, lwd = 2, col = "steelblue")
}
par(op)
mtext(cb_credit(), side = 1, line = -1, outer = TRUE, adj = 1, cex = 0.6)
```

Grey steps are marginal rates, blue lines average rates. The average rate
approaches the top marginal rate only slowly: Australia's 45% top rate gives
an average rate well below 40% even at twice the top threshold.

## When does the average rate reach 20%?

A single number that summarises progressivity: the income at which the band
arithmetic alone takes 20% of the amount. `uniroot()` solves it per schedule.

```{r}
income_at_average <- function(tab, section, target) {
  f <- function(x) cb_tax_from_bands(x, tab, section) / x - target
  top <- max(tab$from[tab$section_id == section], na.rm = TRUE)
  upper <- 100 * max(top, 1)
  if (f(1) >= 0) return(0)          # the first band is already at or above the target
  if (f(upper) < 0) return(NA_real_) # never reached
  uniroot(f, c(1, upper), tol = 0.01)$root
}
overview$income_at_20pct <- round(mapply(function(tab, sec) income_at_average(tab, sec, 0.20),
                                         tables, schedules$section))
overview[, c("country", "currency", "top_rate", "income_at_20pct")]
```

These amounts are in local currency and before any allowance or credit that
sits outside the bands (0 means the first band's rate is already 20% or more,
as in the UK, where the bands start above the Personal Allowance). To compare them across countries, convert with
exchange rates or purchasing-power parities of your choice:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Your own conversion factors: local currency units per US dollar.
lcu_per_usd <- c(USD = 1, GBP = NA, CAD = NA, AUD = NA, INR = NA, SGD = NA, EUR = NA)  # fill in
overview$income_at_20pct_usd <- overview$income_at_20pct / lcu_per_usd[overview$currency]
```

## Combining values and bands: the UK Personal Allowance taper

Tables also hold single values, such as allowances and thresholds. The UK
Personal Allowance of GBP 12,570 is withdrawn by GBP 1 for every GBP 2 of
income above GBP 100,000, which creates a 60% marginal rate between
GBP 100,000 and GBP 125,140. All three figures are in the table:

```{r}
uk <- cb_tax_table("uk")
pa_rows <- uk[uk$section_id == "personal-allowance", c("label", "value", "rate", "source_url")]
pa_rows

pa <- pa_rows$value[pa_rows$label == "Personal Allowance"]
limit <- pa_rows$value[pa_rows$label == "Income limit for the Personal Allowance"]
taper <- pa_rows$rate[grepl("taper", pa_rows$label)]

uk_income_tax <- function(gross) {
  allowance <- pmax(0, pa - taper * pmax(0, gross - limit))
  cb_tax_from_bands(pmax(0, gross - allowance), uk, "income-tax-england")
}
gross <- c(30000, 60000, 100000, 110000, 125140, 150000)
data.frame(gross, tax = uk_income_tax(gross), average = round(uk_income_tax(gross) / gross, 3))
```

The marginal rate, by finite differences:

```{r}
g <- seq(90000, 140000, by = 10)
marginal <- diff(uk_income_tax(g)) / diff(g)
unique(round(marginal, 2))
```

The real HMRC rules also round the allowance and taxable income to whole
pounds and add Scottish and Welsh rates for residents there, so treat this as
the band arithmetic, not a tax return. For complete take-home pay figures,
`cb_net_salary()` calls the same engine as the calculators on calcbloc.com.

## Regional schedules from the API

Regional tables (US states, Canadian provinces, Swiss cantons, Spanish
autonomous communities, ...) are not bundled, to keep the package small. They
come from the CalcBloc API. Without a key the API allows 50 requests a day
and 5 a minute per IP address; the client spaces requests, caches responses
for the session and waits when the server asks it to. A free key
([https://calcbloc.com/developers](https://calcbloc.com/developers?utm_source=calcbloc-r&utm_medium=docs&utm_campaign=itmarkerz-oss)) in `CALCBLOC_API_KEY` raises the limit.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
provinces <- cb_regions("canada")$code
on <- cb_tax_table("canada", region = "on", source = "api")
cb_sections(on, kind = "bands")
cb_tax_from_bands(80000, on, cb_sections(on, kind = "bands")$section_id[1])
```
